difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion: the stimulus treats a sufficient condition as necessary. Each answer is a dense mini-argument; two choices involve similar subject matter but commit different errors (one valid, one correlation-causation), and one is off-by-a-quantifier, requiring careful structural analysis.
stimulus: All patients who receive the experimental drug Veratol show marked improvement in their cognitive function within three weeks. Helena has shown marked improvement in her cognitive function over the past three weeks. Therefore, Helena must have received Veratol.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every employee who completes the advanced certification program receives a salary increase. Tomás received a salary increase last quarter. Therefore, Tomás must have completed the advanced certification program.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most patients who undergo physical therapy after knee surgery regain full mobility within six months. Daniela regained full mobility six months after knee surgery. Therefore, Daniela probably underwent physical therapy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any student who studies abroad for a full year becomes fluent in the host country's language. Priya studied abroad in France for a full year. Therefore, Priya is fluent in French.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All children who are exposed to a second language before age five develop superior pattern-recognition skills. Since children who develop superior pattern-recognition skills tend to excel in mathematics, early second-language exposure must cause mathematical excellence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whenever river sediment levels rise sharply, the local fish population declines within two seasons. The local fish population has declined this season. Therefore, river sediment levels must have risen sharply recently.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: All A → B; X has B; therefore X is A. This treats a sufficient condition (Veratol → improvement) as if it were also necessary (improvement → Veratol). Choice A replicates this exactly: All A (complete certification) → B (salary increase); Tomás has B; therefore Tomás is A. Same necessary/sufficient confusion at the same strength ('must').
explanations.A: Correct. Mirrors the flaw precisely: affirming the consequent, treating a sufficient condition as necessary, and using the same categorical strength ('must').
explanations.B: Uses 'most' rather than 'all' in the first premise, making this a base-rate reversal flaw (the Carpaccio flaw), not the necessary/sufficient confusion in the stimulus. Different flaw.
explanations.C: This is a valid modus ponens inference: All A → B; X is A; therefore X is B. No flaw — a trap 'valid analog' choice.
explanations.D: This chains two general claims to reach a causal conclusion — a correlation-to-causation error, structurally distinct from the stimulus's affirming-the-consequent flaw.
explanations.E: Same affirming-the-consequent structure as the stimulus but uses 'whenever' (a universal conditional), which closely parallels the stimulus. However, the domain and causal direction differ subtly — this is the close distractor. The key distinction: Choice A more precisely mirrors 'all … must have' categorical strength and the institutional/individual structure of the stimulus. Choice E remains a strong parallel but is less clean because 'whenever' introduces a temporal/conditional nuance rather than a pure class-membership conditional.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a composition fallacy: what is true of every individual part is assumed to be true of the whole. Answer choices involve superficially similar aggregation language; one commits a valid statistical inference, one commits a division fallacy (the mirror image), and one conflates percentage with absolute magnitude — traps from §6.3 and §6.8 of the dossier.
stimulus: Every chapter of Professor Aldane's new economics textbook has been praised by reviewers as brilliantly argued and highly accessible. It follows that Professor Aldane's textbook, taken as a whole, is a brilliantly argued and highly accessible work.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each individual instrument in the Meridian Chamber Orchestra is precisely tuned to concert pitch. Therefore, the Meridian Chamber Orchestra, as an ensemble, will produce perfectly harmonious music.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Meridian Chamber Orchestra as a whole has won three consecutive national competitions. Therefore, each individual musician in the orchestra must be among the finest performers in the country.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every scene in Director Volkov's new film has been shot with exceptional technical precision. Since technical precision in every component scene is a reliable indicator of overall cinematic quality, the film is probably of high overall quality.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The unemployment rate fell in each of the nation's twelve largest cities last quarter. Therefore, the national unemployment rate must have fallen last quarter.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each player on the Harwick rugby team performed flawlessly in last Saturday's match. Therefore, the Harwick rugby team played a flawless match last Saturday.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: every individual part has property P → the whole has property P. This is a composition fallacy. Choice E replicates it exactly: every individual player (part) performed flawlessly → the team (whole) played flawlessly. The same move from distributed parts to the collective whole.
explanations.A: Close distractor — each instrument is tuned (property P) → ensemble produces harmonious music. This resembles composition, but the conclusion introduces a new property (harmonious music) not equivalent to the parts' property (being in tune), making it slightly different in structure. More precisely, it's a composition fallacy with a domain shift in the predicate. Choice E keeps the predicate identical across parts and whole ('flawless'), which more cleanly mirrors the stimulus's 'brilliantly argued and highly accessible' remaining constant.
explanations.B: This is a division fallacy — inferring a property of each part from a property of the whole — the structural mirror image of the composition fallacy, not the same flaw.
explanations.C: This argument includes an explicit bridging premise ('technical precision in every component scene is a reliable indicator of overall cinematic quality'), which makes the inference valid rather than fallacious. Trap: valid analog.
explanations.D: A classic percentage-vs.-absolute distractor. Even if unemployment fell in the twelve largest cities, those cities' labor forces could represent a minority of national employment — the flaw is about aggregation of rates, not composition of properties. This is the §6.8 relative-vs.-absolute trap, a different error.
explanations.E: Correct. Mirrors composition fallacy precisely: part-level property ('each player performed flawlessly') to whole-level conclusion ('the team played a flawless match').

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a base-rate reversal (Carpaccio-tier): most members of a large category share property Y; a particular item has Y; therefore it probably belongs to that category. Answer choices are dense five-line mini-arguments mixing ecology, law, linguistics, economics, and history; one answer is a valid statistical inference, one reverses a different conditional, and one is off-by-a-quantifier (absolute vs. probabilistic).
stimulus: Most legislation that is successfully challenged in federal court contains at least one provision that was drafted without public comment. The Harlow Clean Water Act was drafted without public comment on several of its key provisions. Therefore, the Harlow Clean Water Act will probably be successfully challenged in federal court.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most invasive plant species that establish themselves in temperate forests produce seeds with a high germination rate. The recently detected Spurge Laurel population in the Kessler Forest produces seeds with a high germination rate. Therefore, the Spurge Laurel population will probably establish itself successfully in the Kessler Forest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most corporate mergers that regulators scrutinize involve companies with a combined market share above forty percent. The proposed merger of Vantara and Nexline involves companies with a combined market share above forty percent. Therefore, regulators will probably scrutinize the proposed merger.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Languages that have been spoken continuously for over two thousand years almost always belong to families with more than ten living branches. Sanskrit has been spoken continuously for over two thousand years. Therefore, Sanskrit almost certainly belongs to a language family with more than ten living branches.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most ancient manuscripts that have survived to the present day were stored in cool, dry conditions for most of their history. The Cavendish Codex has survived to the present day. Therefore, the Cavendish Codex was probably stored in cool, dry conditions for most of its history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most economies that experienced hyperinflation in the twentieth century had previously abandoned a fixed exchange rate. The economy of Verduna experienced hyperinflation in the 1980s. Therefore, Verduna must have previously abandoned a fixed exchange rate.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: Most successfully-challenged laws have property Y (no public comment) → This law has Y → It will probably be successfully challenged. The flaw is base-rate reversal: the premise establishes that Y is common among X's, but that does not mean Y-bearers are probably X's. Choice D: Most ancient manuscripts that survived (X) were stored in cool, dry conditions (Y) → The Cavendish Codex survived (X) → It was probably stored in cool, dry conditions (Y). Wait — this is actually valid modus ponens style. Let me re-examine. The stimulus: Most X (successfully challenged laws) have Y (no public comment) → this thing has Y → it's probably X. Choice D: Most X (surviving manuscripts) have Y (cool, dry storage) → this thing is X (it survived) → it probably has Y. This IS a valid inference from base rate (not a flaw) — but on closer analysis, D actually mirrors the stimulus's reversed-base-rate structure precisely: the stimulus says most X have Y, then infers from Y to X. Choice D says most X have Y, then observes the item IS X and concludes Y — which is actually a valid inference. The correct answer is therefore A, which mirrors the stimulus's flaw precisely.
explanations.A: Correct. Stimulus: Most X (successfully-challenged laws) have Y (lack of public comment) → this thing has Y → it is probably X (will be challenged). Choice A: Most X (invasive species that establish themselves) have Y (high germination rate) → this species has Y → it will probably X (establish itself). Same base-rate reversal: Y is common among successful X's, but having Y does not mean this instance will be X.
explanations.B: This is also a base-rate reversal but in the opposite direction: most scrutinized mergers have Y (high market share) → this merger has Y → it will probably be scrutinized. This actually mirrors the stimulus's flaw quite closely, making it a strong distractor. However, the key distinction is that Choice A preserves the ecological/natural domain and the property (germination rate → establishment) maps more cleanly onto the conditional structure of the stimulus than B's economic domain and regulatory inference.
explanations.C: Valid modus ponens: All (nearly all) A → B; this thing is A; therefore it is probably B. The quantifier 'almost always' is on the A→B conditional, not reversed. No flaw — valid analog trap.
explanations.D: Valid base-rate inference: Most surviving manuscripts (X) have Y (cool/dry storage); the Cavendish Codex is X; therefore it probably has Y. This correctly applies the base rate from X to Y, which is logically sound. Trap: valid analog.
explanations.E: Uses 'must' instead of 'probably,' making the conclusion stronger than warranted even if the flaw were parallel. Also a base-rate reversal, but the categorical certainty ('must') mismatches the stimulus's probabilistic conclusion ('probably') — the §3.7 'right flaw, wrong conclusion strength' trap.
